items.prompt: A function must materialize k output records. What time lower bound follows immediately under a unit-cost write model?

options.text: Ω(k).
Ω(1) only.
Ω(log k).
No lower bound follows from output.

feedback.reason: Every materialized result record must be written or otherwise produced.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Under the stated unit-cost model, materializing one constant-size record requires at least one write or emission action. Repeating that obligation for k distinct records requires at least k actions, so time is Ω(k). Even an O(1) discovery mechanism cannot bypass work required by the result interface.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: This is a lower bound, not a complete upper bound. Input search, validation or record size may add larger terms.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.omega_1: A constant bound ignores that each of the k required records needs its own materialization action.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.omega_log_k: Only logarithmically many writes cannot explicitly produce k distinct constant-size records under this interface.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero: The contract itself mandates observable output actions even if finding the records required no computation.

items.prompt: Why can an existence query be asymptotically easier than listing every witness?

options.text: The decision problem may stop after one proof, while enumeration must produce all k witnesses.
Existence queries never inspect input.
Listing k witnesses is always O(1).
Decision and enumeration always have identical lower bounds.

feedback.reason: Result contracts create different unavoidable work.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

An existence query returns one bit of information and may stop as soon as a valid witness is proved. Enumeration must continue until all k witnesses are found and then emit them, creating Ω(k) output work. The search phase may still be expensive for either contract, but the mandatory result sizes establish different lower bounds.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Do not transfer a decision algorithm's bound to enumeration without adding complete-discovery and output costs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.existence_no_input: A constant-size answer does not imply constant search; proving absence may still require examining the full input.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.listing_constant: An explicit list performs at least one output action for each of its k witnesses.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_always: Decision and enumeration may share search work, but their mandatory output volumes differ asymptotically.

items.prompt: A function returns a new list containing k matches and uses only constant working state. Which space classification is precise?

options.text: O(k) output space and O(1) auxiliary space.
O(k) auxiliary space only.
The same list counts as both output and auxiliary storage.
All space is O(1).

feedback.reason: Required result storage is output space.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The returned list exists because the result contract requires it, so its k records count as O(k) output space. The function's counters and current cursor remain O(1) auxiliary state. Reporting the roles separately avoids double-counting the same list while still acknowledging that total process memory grows with the result.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Classify storage by purpose, not allocation site: returned representation is output; temporary computation state is auxiliary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.aux_k: The growing list is the required returned value, so its role is output rather than auxiliary working storage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_k: One allocation should not be charged to both categories; report it once as output and keep auxiliary space separate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_constant: Although working state is constant, the returned representation stores k records and therefore grows with k.

items.prompt: A task asks for every unordered pair among n distinct items. What unavoidable output count appears?

options.text: n(n - 1)/2, which is Θ(n²).
n pairs.
n! pairs.
One pair.

feedback.reason: The result size itself is quadratic.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Each unordered pair chooses two distinct items without order, giving C(n,2) = n(n - 1)/2. This is Θ(n²) records. Any algorithm that explicitly materializes every pair therefore needs Ω(n²) time and output space, so an O(n²) implementation can match the unavoidable output bound.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Pair enumeration is not inefficient merely because it is quadratic; the contract itself contains a quadratic number of answers.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear_pairs: Each item participates with many later items, and summing n - 1 through 1 gives a quadratic count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.factorial_pairs: n! counts complete orderings of all items, while this contract chooses only two and ignores their order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_pairs: The request includes every distinct two-item combination rather than one selected pair.

items.prompt: What is the total number of element occurrences across all materialized subsets of n indexed elements?

options.text: n·2^(n - 1), which is Θ(n·2^n).
Exactly 2^n element occurrences.
n².

feedback.reason: Each element appears in exactly half of the 2^n subsets.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Fix one indexed element. The remaining n - 1 elements may vary freely, so exactly 2^(n - 1) subsets contain the fixed element. Repeating this incidence count for all n elements gives n·2^(n - 1) stored element occurrences. Thus representing every subset as its elements needs Θ(n·2^n) output volume, beyond merely counting 2^n subset containers.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Count both result containers and contents. For materialized subsets, total element occurrences dominate the number of subsets by an n factor.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_n_only: 2^n counts subset containers but ignores how many selected elements are stored inside all of them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_squared: A power set contains exponentially many membership patterns, so a polynomial occurrence count cannot describe it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_factorial: A factorial counts ordered arrangements, whereas subset materialization stores unordered membership choices.

items.prompt: Can returning a symbolic generator handle avoid an Ω(k) materialization bound for a contract that explicitly requires all k records stored in memory?

options.text: No. A lazy handle changes the output contract unless the caller accepts streaming or deferred production.
Yes. A pointer always represents all records at zero cost under the same contract.
Every output can be compressed to O(1) without changing semantics.
Output requirements never affect complexity.

feedback.reason: Compression, laziness, and symbolic descriptions can be valid only when the interface permits them.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

A generator handle describes how records may be produced later; it does not place all k records in memory now. If the public contract explicitly requires a fully materialized collection, returning the handle changes observable semantics, including timing, failure and ownership. Laziness or compression is valid only when that alternate representation is accepted by the interface.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Optimization cannot silently weaken the deliverable. First establish whether callers accept streaming, deferred work or a symbolic representation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_same: A pointer to future computation is not the in-memory collection of k records required by the stated contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_compress_any: Arbitrary outputs need not admit a constant-size lossless representation that preserves random access and materialized semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_ignored: Required representation and delivery perform work and therefore impose time and space lower bounds.

items.prompt: A function streams k results one at a time and retains only constant local state. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It performs Ω(k) output work while using O(1) internal auxiliary space.
There is no output because no list is returned.
The function necessarily retains all k results as auxiliary memory.
One-at-a-time emission makes total time O(1).

feedback.reason: Streaming separates output volume from internal materialization.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The producer performs one emission for each of k results, so output work is Ω(k). Because the sink consumes each record before the next is retained, the producer can reuse O(1) local state and avoid an O(k) in-memory list. Streaming changes peak storage, not the logical result count or number of delivery actions.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Report producer auxiliary space separately from downstream buffering. O(1) holds only if the streaming interface and consumer do not require retaining all records.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_output: Yielding records one at a time is still observable output and occurs k times even without a returned list.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.aux_k: Incremental consumption permits the producer to discard each record, so it need not retain all k as working memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_constant: One-at-a-time delivery still executes k emissions and cannot complete in constant total time.

items.prompt: Does proving an Ω(k) output lower bound prove that every O(k²) algorithm is optimal?

options.text: No. The lower bound only proves at least linear-in-k work; an O(k²) algorithm may contain avoidable overhead.
Yes. Any algorithm above the lower bound is optimal.
Yes, because output-sensitive problems ignore computation.
No lower bounds can ever support optimality claims.

feedback.reason: An algorithm is output-optimal only when its upper bound matches the required-output lower bound, possibly plus unavoidable input work.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Ω(k) says every correct materializer needs at least linear work in result count. An O(k²) upper bound is still a factor k above that evidence and may contain avoidable comparisons or copying. Optimality requires a matching upper and lower bound, commonly Θ(n + k) when input examination is also unavoidable.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: A lower bound certifies optimality only when the implemented upper bound matches it under the same variables, model and result contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_any: Being above a lower bound is necessary but not sufficient; an unexplained asymptotic gap can still be improved.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_output: Output sensitivity includes required emission but does not excuse avoidable search, duplication or processing overhead.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_lower: When an algorithm's upper bound matches a valid lower bound, the pair can prove asymptotic optimality.

items.prompt: An algorithm scans all n inputs and returns no matches, so k = 0. Can its time still be O(n)?

options.text: Yes. Output size can be zero while input examination remains necessary.
No. Zero output forces O(1) time.
No. Zero output implies O(n²).
Time always equals k.

feedback.reason: Output lower bounds are only one component of total work.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

To prove there are no matches, the algorithm may still need to inspect all n input records. The output contribution k is zero, but the discovery contribution remains Θ(n), so a tight bound such as Θ(n + k) becomes Θ(n). Output size supplements the workload model; it does not replace input work.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Test output-sensitive formulas at k = 0. A claimed O(k) algorithm is suspicious when absence still requires reading the input.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_zero: Zero output does not provide a certificate of absence; the algorithm may still scan every candidate input.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.must_quadratic: No result-size rule turns an empty result into quadratic work; the actual discovery algorithm determines that term.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_equals_time: Output-sensitive bounds combine discovery and delivery, so time commonly depends on both n and k.

items.prompt: Which statements about output-sensitive lower bounds are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Materializing k constant-size results requires Ω(k) time.
Retaining k constant-size results requires Ω(k) output space.
A tight algorithm may need an additional input-processing term such as O(n + k).
Output size can always be ignored when stating time.

feedback.reason: Output-sensitive analysis combines unavoidable emission with any necessary discovery cost.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Materializing k constant-size records performs at least k writes and retaining them stores at least k records. Those Ω(k) terms coexist with any necessary input processing, so Θ(n + k) may be tight for a scan-and-report algorithm. Claiming output is free would permit an upper bound smaller than the work the interface visibly performs.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Accept write, storage and additional input terms. Reject `output_free` because it contradicts the materialized result contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_free: Ignoring k can advertise fewer operations or bytes than are required merely to construct and retain the result.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.input_term: Finding or proving results can require scanning input.

items.prompt: Which tasks can have inherently superlinear materialized output? Select all that apply.

options.text: Return all unordered pairs of n items.
Return every subset of n items.
Return every permutation of n items.
Return one boolean saying whether a duplicate exists.

feedback.reason: Enumeration contracts can force polynomial, exponential, or factorial output.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

All unordered pairs contain Θ(n²) records. All subsets contain 2^n containers and Θ(n·2^n) stored elements when materialized. All permutations contain n! sequences and Θ(n·n!) elements. The duplicate-existence task returns one boolean, so its output is constant-size even if discovery still processes n inputs.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Accept the three enumeration tasks. Reject the decision task because witness count and answer representation are different contracts.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.exists_duplicate: The required result is one boolean, so its materialized output does not grow even though the search may.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_subsets: There are 2^n subsets and Θ(n·2^n) total elements.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_permutations: There are n! outputs of length n.

items.prompt: Which storage counts as output rather than auxiliary space? Select all that apply.

options.text: A list explicitly required and returned by the function.
A required result file containing all records.
A deduplication set discarded before return.
Active call frames.

feedback.reason: Role, not allocation time, determines output classification.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The returned list and required result file are the representations delivered to the caller, so they count as output storage. A discarded deduplication set and active recursion frames exist only to compute that result and are auxiliary. Allocation timing or whether a structure temporarily contains candidate answers does not change its semantic role.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Classify by ownership at the interface boundary: delivered representation is output; discarded working state is auxiliary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.temporary_set: Because the set is discarded rather than returned, it supports computation and counts as auxiliary working memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.recursion_stack: Active frames exist to execute recursive calls and are not part of the required result representation.

items.prompt: Which advertised bounds are incomplete or impossible under the stated contract? Select all that apply.

options.text: Return all Θ(n²) pairs in O(n) time.
Materialize every subset in O(2^n) time while each subset is stored as its elements.
Report k matches after a full scan in O(n + k) time.
Store every permutation while claiming O(1) output space.

feedback.reason: A claimed upper bound must be at least large enough to represent the required result.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

All Θ(n²) pairs cannot be explicitly written in O(n) time. Materialized subsets store Θ(n·2^n) element occurrences, so O(2^n) omits an n factor under that representation. Storing all permutations requires Θ(n·n!) output space, not O(1). By contrast, O(n + k) for a full scan plus k constant-time appends includes both discovery and output.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Accept the bounds smaller than their required representation. Reject `report_matches_n_k` because it matches the stated scan-and-report workload.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.report_matches_n_k: The n term covers the full scan and the k term covers one append per match, so the bound is compatible.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_pairs_linear: The algorithm cannot write the output that quickly.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_subsets_two_n: The total emitted element count is Θ(n·2^n).

items.prompt: Arrange the process for deriving an output lower bound.

elements.text: Define one output record and its representation cost.
Bound the maximum or actual number k of required records.
Conclude Ω(k) writes and, when retained, Ω(k) output space.
Compare the candidate upper bound with input and output lower bounds.

feedback.reason: Output-sensitive reasoning starts from the required representation.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The record representation determines the cost of producing one result. Counting how many records the contract requires then yields a write and retention lower bound. Only after those obligations are explicit can the candidate's discovery and overhead be compared against them.

items: Define one required output record and its representation cost.
Bound the number k of records the contract may require.
Derive Ω(k) emissions and, when retained, Ω(k) output storage for constant-size records.
Compare the candidate upper bound with both input-processing and output lower bounds.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: If records have size s rather than constant size, replace k with total representation volume instead of assuming one unit per record.

items.prompt: Arrange the verification of a claimed O(n + k) reporting algorithm.

elements.text: Verify input discovery work is O(n).
Verify each of k results is emitted with O(1) additional work.
Check that no result or input region is repeatedly rescanned.
Compare the upper bound with Ω(n) discovery and Ω(k) output obligations.

feedback.reason: The expression is tight only when hidden work does not multiply n or k.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

First establish that discovery visits the input only linearly. Then prove each result adds constant work and no candidate region or emitted record is revisited in a nested fashion. If the problem also requires Ω(n) inspection and Ω(k) emission, the verified O(n + k) upper bound matches those obligations.

items: Verify that discovery performs O(n) total input work.
Verify that each of k outputs adds O(1) work.
Exclude hidden rescans or per-result passes that would multiply n or k.
Match O(n + k) against the applicable Ω(n) discovery and Ω(k) output lower bounds.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: A syntactic scan plus append is insufficient evidence if the append copies a growing collection or the scan restarts for each match.

items.prompt: A reporting algorithm scans n records once and appends each of k matches with O(1) work. Select time, auxiliary space excluding output, and output space.
constraints: No other growing structure is used.

feedback.reason: The scan and output writes are separate additive work.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The single pass examines n records, contributing Θ(n). Each of k matches is appended with O(1) work, contributing Θ(k), so total time is Θ(n + k). Only counters and the current record remain as O(1) auxiliary state. The returned collection retains k records and therefore occupies Θ(k) output space.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: The additive expression is tight when the scan is necessary and each output append is constant-time; neither term should be relabeled as the other's storage.

items.prompt: A function materializes every unordered pair of n elements. Select pair count, time lower bound, and output-space lower bound.
constraints: Each pair is stored as one constant-size record.

feedback.reason: There are n(n - 1)/2 pairs.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Choosing two distinct elements without order gives C(n,2) = n(n - 1)/2 = Θ(n²) pairs. Writing every constant-size pair requires Ω(n²) time, and retaining them requires Ω(n²) output space. These are lower bounds from representation alone, before any extra discovery or sorting.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: An O(n²) pair generator may be asymptotically optimal because its output already contains Θ(n²) records.

items.prompt: A function materializes all n! permutations, each of length n. Select output count, time lower bound, and output-space lower bound.

feedback.reason: There are n! outputs and each contains n elements.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

There are n! distinct full permutations. Each materialized permutation stores n elements, so the total representation contains n·n! element occurrences. Under unit-cost element writes, time is Ω(n·n!) and retained output space is Ω(n·n!), not merely Ω(n!) containers.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Record count and record size both matter. Treating each length-n permutation as a constant-size output loses a factor of n.

items.prompt: Two sorted lists of lengths n and m are scanned to report all k common-value occurrences with one linear merge. Select time, auxiliary space excluding output, and output space.
constraints: Each input pointer moves only forward and each reported occurrence is appended once.

feedback.reason: The merge discovers candidates in linear input work and emits k results.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Two monotone pointers advance through lists of lengths n and m without retreating, so discovery performs O(n + m) total pointer steps. Emitting k common occurrences adds O(k), yielding O(n + m + k) time. The merge retains only two pointers and current values, so auxiliary space is O(1), while the returned results occupy O(k) output space.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: The bound assumes duplicate semantics are defined and each required occurrence can be emitted in O(1); a cross-product of duplicate groups would change k accordingly.

items.prompt: A function enumerates every subset of n elements and stores each subset as its elements. Select subset count and total materialized output volume.
constraints: Each indexed element appears in exactly half of all subsets.

feedback.reason: Counting subsets alone understates materialization cost.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The power set contains 2^n subset containers. For any fixed element, the other n - 1 memberships vary freely, so that element appears in 2^(n - 1) subsets. Across n elements, materialized contents total n·2^(n - 1) = Θ(n·2^n) occurrences, which dominates container count.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Distinguish enumerating subset identities from storing each subset's elements. The latter has an unavoidable extra n factor in total volume.
